extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator / general literate public; aspiring essayists and moralists
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and exemplars for composing short moral/literary essays and epistolary pieces—showing how to use novelty, imagery, satire, classical quotation, and rhetorical taxonomy to engage readers. Includes sample letters, translations, and satirical anecdotes as models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Force of Novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: "the Force of Novelty" — novelty is the primary source of admiration and the power that awakens desire, enhances delight, kindles anger, provokes envy, inspires horror; passion is usually the effect of surprize and ceases with novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use surprising or new elements to awaken emotions and sustain reader interest; novelty is particularly effective at first appearance of truth or beauty. Example uses: contrasting youthful delight with aged satiety; caution that novelty is transient and must be managed so the mind does not move on prematurely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty as engine of intellectual pursuit
rubrics_metrics.description: "That which makes Men willing to undergo the Fatigues of Philosophical Disquisitions, is not so much the Greatness of objects as their Novelty."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting difficult or abstract subjects, foreground what is new or unexpected to motivate readers' attention. However, be wary: novelty can make writers impatient of sustained inquiry ('We see a little, presume a great deal, and so jump to the Conclusion').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ridiculous imagery in serious speculation
rubrics_metrics.description: The author criticises a correspondent's introduction by an image he calls "too ridiculous in so serious and noble a Speculation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match tone and imagery to the seriousness of the theme. Moralizing on trivial objects (snuff-box, periwig) can be clever, but incongruous or ludicrous images risk undermining the argument's dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contrasts of age to explicate feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast stages of life: "The Child... the Youth... the Man... old Age" to show how novelty and appetite change over a life-course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure character or argument by juxtaposing life-stages to illustrate shifts in appetite, pleasure, and perception; useful for explaining psychological causes of behaviour and for evoking pathos or irony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terse, repetitive Q&A for comedic/satirical effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Series of short questions answered uniformly with 'No.' (e.g., the young woman's letter about Mr. Fondle with repeated single-word answers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ brief, deadpan replies and repetition to satirize naivety, self-deception, or folly; the repeated terse answer becomes a comic device that exposes the querent's faults without explicit sermonizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and freshness in reporting / topical pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: "A Piece of News loses its Flavour when it hath been an Hour in the Air... I love... to have it fresh from the Tree; and to convey it to my Friends before it is faded."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing newsy or topical material, prioritise freshness, rapid sourcing, and immediacy. Speed and being first (coffee-house reporting, forestalling the post) increase perceived value; freshness parallels the 'novelty' that pleases readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use detailed sensory and place-specific description in letters/epistles
rubrics_metrics.description: Long epistolary description of gardens, walks, jessamines, peach trees, and made-up 'walks for two' used to convey longing and imagined companionship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground emotional states in concrete sensory detail and specific landscape features; imaginated, carefully-rendered settings (paths, arbors, fruit-trees) make longing and solitude believable and poignant in epistolary or descriptive passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use classical quotation and translation for authority and style
rubrics_metrics.description: Presentation and praise of a translation of Cato's speech for 'Conciseness, Purity, and Elegance of Phrase.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intersperse classical references or concise translations to lend gravity, cultivate elegance, and situate an essay within learned tradition. A well-chosen classical passage can concentrate and elevate an argument or meditation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirize entitlement via enumerated absurd petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Long catalogue of whimsical/absurd petitions and memorials (requests for offices and honours based on trivial or ridiculous services) used to mock pretensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expose social folly by compiling a series of exaggerated or ludicrous claims; the cumulative effect of enumerated absurdities makes satire sharper and reveals the gap between merit and entitlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organise argument by taxonomic division
rubrics_metrics.description: Opening move: 'Mankind is divided into two Parts, the Busie and the Idle. The Busie World may be divided into the Virtuous and the Vicious...' used to structure the ensuing comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame complex topics by clear classificatory schemes (dividing the subject into categories) to guide the reader through comparisons and moral weighing; useful for systematic essays that compare virtues and vices or alternative courses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support moral claims with authoritative exempla and quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of St. Paul's catalogue of sufferings, Cardinal Woolsey's complaint, and other named authorities to illustrate moral points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bolster ethical or philosophical claims by citing recognized authorities or exemplars; specific quotations and allusions give rhetorical weight and situate personal argument within a larger moral discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use enumerated catalogues of toil to dramatize vice or virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed listing of the Miser's pains ('In journeying often; in Perils of Water, in Perils of Robbers... in Hunger and Thirst, in Fastings often') to demonstrate the costliness of vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ vivid enumerations of trials, dangers, or labours to dramatize the burdens attached to a pursuit (vice or virtue); such catalogues increase rhetorical force and help readers feel the comparative weight of choices.
